verdicts.why: In the sense 'be valid, applicable, or true' the word states that a rule or condition holds, and takes no side on whether that is good or bad.
An era of history marked by some feature is a plain period label, with no attitude toward the period named.
A prolonged period of time is a plain measure of duration; the length is the meaning, not an attitude beyond it.
Freedom from work or strain names a state without praising or blaming the person in it; any idleness reading belongs to the referent, not the word.
Financial comfort is named plainly here; the word describes the circumstances without judging the person who enjoys them.
A provable concept is a neutral epistemic label; choosing 'fact' asserts truth but expresses no attitude toward the thing it is true of.
To increase or develop is a plain statement of change in amount or degree, with no approval or contempt attached.
Obtaining points or advantages is described flatly; the outcome may be welcome, but the verb itself does not judge the gainer.
Earning money in a transaction or as wages is a neutral description of income, not a comment on how it was come by.
Increasing body weight is stated as a plain change in measure; the verb carries no attitude toward the person, unlike words such as 'bloat'.
A rise in rate or price is a plain market description and takes no side on whether the rise is welcome.
Reaching a destination, real or abstract, is described without any judgement of the traveller or the goal.
A device that signals an undesirable event is a plain name for an object; the undesirable event is the referent, not a stance in the word.
The condition of understanding is a neutral cognitive term in this sense, and the word says nothing about the value of what is understood.
Preparing or positioning something for action is a plain description of arrangement, with no attitude toward the actor or the object.
Laying eggs is a flat biological description with no judgement in it.
A unit of corporate stock is a technical financial term and carries no attitude toward its holder.
The cutting blade of a plough is a plain name for a tool part, with no judgement attached.
A decorative knot of ribbons is a plain object name; any prettiness belongs to the thing, not to the word's stance.
The front of a vessel or aircraft is a neutral technical term with no attitude in it.
The stringed-instrument bow is a plain name for an object and judges nothing.
Something curved in shape is a purely descriptive term with no approval or dismissal in it.
A performer's acknowledgement of applause is a plain description of a stage convention, not a comment on the performer.
A bow stroke on a stringed instrument is a neutral technical term with no stance toward the player.
In the legal sense of disobedience to a court, 'contempt' is a term of art naming an offence; the offence is a bad referent, and the word does not add the speaker's own scorn beyond that meaning.
